one_liner: Public-domain xoshiro/xoroshiro PRNG family, faster than std::mt19937_64, not cryptographically secure.
what_it_does: A family of small, fast, non-cryptographic pseudorandom generators (xoshiro256++, xoshiro256**, xoroshiro128++, and 32/16-bit variants) distributed as single self-contained C source files, one per algorithm variant, rather than a library with one entry point. Each file exposes a `next()` function returning the next 64- (or 32/16-) bit word plus `jump()`/`long_jump()` functions that advance the state by a fixed 2^128/2^192 stride to create non-overlapping streams for parallel use. Seeding is manual: you fill the global state array yourself, and the author recommends expanding a single 64-bit seed through SplitMix64 rather than seeding with the target algorithm's own output.
how_it_is_fast: Each generator keeps 128-1024 bits of state and does a handful of XOR/shift/rotate ops plus one integer add or multiply per call ('scrambled linear' generators), versus MT19937-64's much larger ~2.5KB state array and heavier tempering step. On the project's own shootout (gcc 12.2.1, -fno-unroll-loops, i7-12700KF), xoshiro256++ produces 64 bits in 0.75ns/0.34 cycles-per-byte against 1.36ns/0.62 cycles-per-byte for a reference MT19937-64 C implementation, about 1.8x. The small register-sized state also lets AVX2-vectorized builds run several lanes in parallel (xoshiro256+ drops to 0.19ns/64 bits at 8-wide), though the shootout table itself deliberately avoids -march=native.
when_to_use: Non-cryptographic Monte Carlo / simulation / scientific-computing code generating large volumes of 64-bit random values where throughput matters
Need many independent parallel random streams (per-thread, per-worker) - jump()/long_jump() give cheap non-overlapping subsequences without reseeding
Vendoring a tiny, public-domain, single-file generator into a codebase - already the default behind Julia's Random, Rust's SmallRng, Java 17+ java.util.random, .NET 6, Lua, and GNU Fortran
Replacing std::mt19937_64 in hot loops where its large state and tempering overhead show up in profiles
Constrained/embedded targets needing a very small generator - xoroshiro128+ is used in Mbed/Zephyr, and 32/16-bit variants exist for smaller word sizes
when_not_to_use: Any cryptographic use (keys, nonces, tokens) - explicitly not cryptographically secure; use a CSPRNG (ChaCha20, AES-CTR) instead
Need a zero-effort drop-in C++ <random> UniformRandomBitGenerator - these are raw C source files, not a std::mt19937_64-compatible class; you wire up seeding and state ownership yourself

Statistical-test purism: xoshiro/xoroshiro fail a handful of specialized tests despite passing BigCrush overall (e.g. xoroshiro128+ shows a detectable low-bit Hamming-weight dependency after ~5TB of output)
Code that depends on MT19937's enormous 2^19937-1 period for theoretical guarantees - xoshiro256++'s 2^256-1 period is smaller, though still astronomically large for practical use
Wanting a conventional maintained repo with issue tracker/CI - this is a hand-maintained personal website distributing source files, not a git project

integration.dependencies: none for the core generator (stdint.h only); the separate f2x.c tool is only needed to compute custom/arbitrary jump distances
integration.min_toolchain: any C compiler with stdint.h (C99-era); no build system - compile or #include the .c file directly
integration.platforms: any platform with the needed integer width (16/32/64-bit variants provided); the reference code has no SIMD/architecture-specific intrinsics, though hand-vectorized AVX2 builds are discussed on the page
integration.thread_safety: not thread-safe as shipped - state is a plain global array (e.g. `static uint64_t s[4]`) with no locking; give each thread its own state instance, offset via jump()/long_jump() for non-overlapping streams
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same 'call next() for the next block of random bits' shape as advancing std::mt19937_64, but not a C++ UniformRandomBitGenerator class; no built-in seeding routine or <random>-compatible wrapper is provided

gotchas: Must not seed the state directly from a plain counter/timestamp - guidance on the page is to expand the seed through a different-family generator (SplitMix64), or output quality suffers
xoroshiro128+'s low output bits have a detectable linear dependency (fails specific tests after ~5TB of output) - use xoroshiro128++ or xoroshiro128** if the low bits matter
jump()/long_jump() only give fixed 2^128/2^192 strides; arbitrary jump distances require the separate f2x.c polynomial tool
The all-zero state is a fixed point and invalid for these generators - any custom seeding routine must avoid it
verified_claims_summary: On the project's own shootout table (gcc 12.2.1, -fno-unroll-loops, no -march=native, i7-12700KF @3.6GHz), xoshiro256++ emits 64 random bits in 0.75ns/0.34 cycles-per-byte versus 1.36ns/0.62 cycles-per-byte for a reference Matsumoto-Nishimura MT19937-64 C implementation (not std::mt19937_64 itself), about 1.8x faster; per the record's verification notes this is corroborated by a peer-reviewed 2021 ACM TOMS paper (arXiv:1805.01407, whose title/authors/thesis I confirmed but whose Table 1 numbers were not visible on the abstract page I fetched) reporting 0.86ns vs 2.19ns on different hardware.
status_note: Hand-maintained personal website (not a git repo) rather than a conventional software release, marked 'active' with the xoshiro256plusplus.c file last modified June 2026; each generator is a single copy-pasteable public-domain/0BSD-licensed C file, consistent with its 'copyable' usability rating.
